facts.detail: Customers should receive clear speed information when buying broadband.
Estimated busy-time speeds cover 8-10pm for home services and 12-2pm for business services.
Providers should give a personalised minimum guaranteed speed, with superfast estimates based on the line capability.
If a provider-network speed problem cannot be fixed within 30 days, the customer must be offered penalty-free exit.

guard_streams.write_limit: Contractual speed information and remedies do not prove exact current parcel performance.

facts.detail: Ofcom advises Ethernet-connected testing because Wi-Fi can slow the signal.
Customers should check the contract or ask the provider to identify the expected speed.
After sale, providers should send speed estimates, relevant policies and instructions for speeds below the guarantee.
The speed-code exit right extends to products linked financially, contractually or technically.

guard_streams.write_limit: Testing advice and contract records are not accepted parcel measurements.

facts.detail: Ofcom advises several speed tests over multiple days and at different times.
Electrical devices and wireless emitters can interfere with routers, so placement matters.
An older router or repeated disconnections may justify discussing an upgrade with the provider.
Password protection helps prevent nearby unauthorised use that can reduce speed and create security risk.

guard_streams.write_limit: Home-network troubleshooting does not establish access-network availability or parcel speed.

facts.detail: A direct Ethernet connection should be faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi.
For phone-line broadband, the main socket, a microfilter and avoiding long extension leads can reduce interference.
Code signatories commit to give the estimated speed range in writing at contract start.
Signatories commit to explain technical speed factors and maintain robust speed-problem processes.

guard_streams.write_limit: In-home improvements and voluntary-code commitments cannot populate exact parcel fields.

guard_streams.source: Ofcom universal service obligations and Connected Nations Spring 2026

facts.detail: Universal service obligations create a safety net for requesting a minimum set of affordable communications services.
BT and KCOM are the designated broadband and telephony universal service providers.
Broadband USO legislation was introduced in 2018 and implemented through Ofcom conditions in March 2020.
The broadband USO right concerns at least 10 Mbit/s download and 1 Mbit/s upload, subject to eligibility and affordability requirements.

guard_streams.write_limit: A right to request a qualifying connection is not evidence that a parcel currently has one.

facts.detail: The business code aims to provide accurate and transparent standard-broadband speed information at point of sale.
Signatories provide expected download and upload estimates before purchase and relevant speed information in writing after sale.
Signatories must manage business speed problems effectively and assist resolution.
The code provides a penalty-free exit below the minimum guarantee after attempted resolution, while some provisions vary by technology.

guard_streams.write_limit: Business-code estimates and remedies do not prove parcel serviceability or live throughput.

facts.detail: Ofcom published the record-low complaints update on 23 July 2026.
The latest figures cover January to March 2026.
Broadband complaints fell from a 2011 peak of 40 per 100,000 customers to six per 100,000 in Q1 2026.
Ofcom says complaint data should be considered alongside price, availability and quality when comparing providers.

guard_streams.write_limit: Aggregate complaints are provider-level evidence and cannot establish parcel coverage or performance.

facts.detail: Signed-up broadband and landline providers pay compensation automatically in qualifying cases.
Delayed-repair compensation applies when service is not fully fixed after two full working days following a reported loss.
A missed engineer appointment or cancellation with less than 24 hours notice qualifies under the scheme.
Failure to start a new service on the promised date qualifies for daily compensation.

guard_streams.write_limit: Compensation eligibility confirms a remedy, not current network availability at a parcel.

facts.detail: Gigaclear is the awarded supplier for East Gloucestershire.
The contract value is £16 million.
The award targets around 4,400 hard-to-reach premises.
The contract was signed in February 2024 and premise scope can change after detailed planning or for technical reasons.

guard_streams.write_limit: Award scope and anticipated access do not prove current parcel orderability.

facts.detail: Wessex Internet is the awarded supplier for North Dorset.
The contract value is £6 million.
The contract targets more than 7,000 premises.
The contract was signed on 25 August 2022 and requires detailed planning and physical build before service access.

guard_streams.write_limit: A regional award and build plan cannot identify delivered parcels.
